title: Westbrook City Council — Regular Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. This was an unusually long meeting (just over three hours); summarization necessarily condenses and selects, especially for the extended Student Transit Pass debate. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Gary Rairdon. Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: Mayor’s Message
National Night Out, Barry Dodd Tribute, Hannaford Crosswalk Preview & Food Security Grants
Discussion Summary

National Night Out is Tuesday, August 4, 5–7 PM at St. Anthony's Church (268 Brown St.). It offers free food, games, a bounce house, and an appearance by the Portland Sea Dogs' mascot, Slugger. The Facilities & Streets Committee meeting immediately following this Council meeting would take up the private-ways policy review flagged at the June 15 meeting. There would be a public comment opportunity there.

Mayor Morse gave an extended tribute to Barry Dodd, the departing Digital Creative Services Administrator. Dodd is leaving after 12 years for a role with the City of Biddeford. The Mayor credited him with modernizing the City's broadcast/communications operations. Examples included the “We Lit the City” holiday-lights video (a Silver Circle Award winner) and a U2 tribute band performance at the downtown parking garage's opening. Dodd's own farewell letter was read into the record during public comment.

The Mayor previewed Order 2026-87. It is a $450,000 project to add a new crosswalk and Americans with Disabilities Act improvements at the William Clark Drive/Hannaford Drive intersection. The City is seeking $225,000 in Portland Area Comprehensive Transportation System (PACTS) Urban Partnership Initiative funding. The project addresses a long-standing resident complaint about pedestrians getting a “walk” signal at the same time as a left-turn green arrow. Westbrook's application ranked first among the sub-region's submissions.

Applications are open for the Westbrook Food Security Grant Program. Awards are $2,500–$5,000 for charitable/nonprofit organizations assisting food-insecure residents. Applications are due 4 PM Friday, August 21.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.
Action Items
None.
Orders of the Day — Second & Final Reading
Orders 2026-81, -82, -83 — Colonial Road Driveway, SCBA Compressor & Bucket Truck (Consent)
Discussion Summary

All three were first read July 20, 2026 (a first reading is the first of two required votes). They are the $24,300 Colonial Road pump station driveway repair, the $107,170 Fire Department SCBA (self-contained breathing apparatus) air compressor, and the $170,519.85 replacement aerial bucket truck. This is the final reading, the last and binding vote. Resident Larry McWilliams questioned the bucket truck's cost and the rust issue on the old unit. City Administrator Angela Holmes clarified that this is a Public Services (not Fire Department) vehicle. Director Eric Dudley said rust is concentrated around the painted-steel storage boxes. He explained that the new truck uses a gas engine rather than diesel specifically because stationary diesel “regen” cycles “can feel pretty toxic” and are difficult for crews to work around. Resident Joyce Van Waltham asked about an electric alternative. Staff said no electric aerial-bucket truck exists at the required power/hydraulic capacity.
Key Decisions
Passed together by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-84: Student Transit Pass Program — Final Passage (5–2)

This was by far the evening's dominant item, drawing dozens of speakers and roughly two and a half hours of discussion. Mayor Morse gave an extended argument for treating the program as a formal one-year pilot. He cited data that roughly 56% of Westbrook's student population lives below the poverty line, versus about 8% of the community overall. He also stressed that the pay-per-ride cost structure caps the cost at $34,000/year.

Point/Counterpoint — is the bus-pass funding separable from the Monroe Avenue route change? Councilor Chau argued throughout that the Council was being asked to fund the pass program while a closely tied (but formally separate) Metro route change went ahead without enough ridership data. The change is a new Route 3 stop at Monroe Avenue and Stroudwater Street. He canvassed the Monroe/Glenwood neighborhood over the weekend. He reported broad support for the pass itself but unease about the specific route change. City Solicitor Cameron Ferrante confirmed that the Council has no authority over Metro's bus routes.
“We're not asking to say no, no buses, no passes... We're saying, can you let us know how many kids will use this?”

Mike Tremblay, Metro's Director of Transit Development, explained that the Monroe Avenue alignment was the primary option for getting a stop within roughly a quarter-mile of the high school without a major route deviation. He later agreed that the walking distance from the Hannaford stop is similar. He said Metro was open to alternatives once school starts. Public comment ran heavily split. School Committee members, housing-sector professionals, and several residents spoke or wrote in support. They cited equity and a University of Minnesota study. The study found that free transit passes reduced excused absences 11.5% overall and 37.6% in a school's walk zone. Monroe/Glenwood-area residents raised a consistent set of concerns: lack of advance neighborhood notice, narrow-street traffic safety, and a shared sense that the route was being finalized without ridership evidence. The response was that a school survey (about 53% said they would ride) and estimates of about 100 available students, perhaps 50 riders, had effectively demonstrated the need.
“If you are voting not about the bus route, I would request that you make that very clear... please don't rush through this and make sure that you have the information you need.”
Key Decisions

[2:36:37] Councilor Chau's amendment to send the Monroe Avenue route discussion to committee failed, 2–5. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Gary Rairdon. For: Victor Chau, Gary Rairdon. Against: Brian McCambridge, Michael Shaughnessy, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Jennifer Munro.

Order 2026-84 then passed [2:40:15], 5–2. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Brian McCambridge. For: Brian McCambridge, Michael Shaughnessy, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Jennifer Munro. Against: Victor Chau, Gary Rairdon.

Councilor McCambridge asked the administration to prioritize police traffic enforcement on Monroe Avenue and to consider suspending the route's summer-schedule operation. Mayor Morse replied that suspending it was “absolutely possible.” He said Metro's data on non-student riders could inform that decision. There was no response on enforcement.
Resolve 2026-15: Riverwalk North Trail Alignment
Garfield Street Alignment Endorsed Over Abutter Objections
Found on page 67 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This resolve (a formal statement or decision by the Council) endorses extending the Riverwalk North trail from the pedestrian bridge to Garfield Street. Staff and consultants recommended this alignment over an alternative extending to Mentor Street. The Mentor Street option would require an additional 360 feet of boardwalk through more sensitive wetland. The City retains the right to extend the trail along Water Street in the future.

Abutting (neighboring) property owner Deborah “Jean” Bryanton (57 Dana Court) spoke at length against the project generally. She said every abutter she has talked to is opposed. She raised questions about maintenance cost, trespassing, policing, lighting, winter maintenance, shoreland zoning, and wildlife impact. A letter from Sarah Hancock cited nearly twenty years of abutter opposition. It echoed similar long-standing concerns, including unresolved property-boundary and construction-liability questions. Countering this, a letter from Garfield Street residents Allison and Dan Peterson backed the Garfield Street alignment specifically. Longtime riverside resident Heather Chandler wrote in support of extending the trail.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Action Items
None.
New Business — Orders (One Reading Required)
Order 2026-85 — Confirming Melissa Littlehale as Tax Collector
Found on page 80 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order confirms Melissa Littlehale as Tax Collector. She joined the City in late June. She has 20+ years of accounting/finance/payroll/tax experience. She previously operated her own law practice in estate planning and real estate. She has a Juris Doctor (law degree) from the University of Maine School of Law, and she is a U.S. Air Force veteran. The order also formally recommits outstanding tax collection duties from outgoing Interim Finance Director Laura King. A floor amendment (a change made during the meeting) corrected a typo in the covered tax-year range (April 1, 2020 to April 1, 2021).
Key Decisions
Floor amendment passed by show of hands, none opposed. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Anna Turcotte.
Order as amended passed by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-86 — Criminal Forfeiture Assets
Found on page 94 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order accepts $1,225 in cash (to the Police Department's forfeiture revenue line) and a Ruger 9mm and Canik 9mm handgun (to be destroyed). They were forfeited from a Westbrook Aggravated Drug Trafficking investigation, per order of the Maine Attorney General's Office.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-87 — Hannaford Drive PACTS/UPI Crosswalk Application
Found on page 99 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order endorses the City's PACTS Urban Partnership Initiative application for the Hannaford Drive crosswalk project described in the Mayor's Message. Councilor Chau asked whether this would eliminate the conflict between pedestrians and left turns happening at the same time. Director Dudley explained that state design rules for principal arterial highways don't allow an exclusive pedestrian phase here (unlike downtown's Bridge/Main St. intersection). A pedestrian “lead phase” was already added as an interim measure.
Key Decisions
Passed 6–0 (Councilor Faulkingham recorded absent for this one roll call). Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-88 — Repealing the Local Motorized Scooter Ordinance
Found on page 105 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order repeals the City's local motorized-scooter prohibition in Chapter 310. That prohibition is an ordinance, meaning a city law. Regulation and enforcement would be deferred entirely to state statute. This follows the July 6 Public Safety Committee discussion. Councilor Chau asked that the City help publicize applicable state laws (minimum age 16, driver's license required). He cited a similar public-education campaign in Scarborough.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
New Business — Orders (First Reading, Two Readings Required)
Order 2026-89 — Replacement Pump Station Doors
Found on page 108 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order authorizes $8,033.03 for two replacement heavy metal doors (with frames, installed) at the Gray Goose and Brydon Farms pump stations. They come from Kamco Supply Corp., a sole-source vendor (one bought from without competitive bidding).
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous show of hands (first reading). Moved by Brian McCambridge, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-90 — Forestry Mulcher Rental & Vendor List Amendment
Found on page 112 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This order authorizes a $7,500 rental of a forestry mulcher/excavator attachment from National Attachments Inc. of Gorham. It would clear vegetation along hard-to-access cross-country sewer lines. It also includes a related amendment adding that company to the annual vendor list.
Key Decisions
Passed by unanimous show of hands (first reading). Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
Second Public Comment & Closing
Police Response Praise, Ward 2 Canvassing & Adjournment
Discussion Summary

Councilor Turcotte described witnessing police respond to a mental-health crisis near her home over the weekend. She praised the department's calm, professional handling. Councilor Chau described his weekend door-to-door canvass of Monroe Avenue residents. He relayed their separate concerns about rising tax bills and hoped new rental-vehicle-registration revenue could help offset future increases. There were no referrals, no committee report updates, and no executive session (a closed, private session allowed by state law for certain topics). The meeting adjourned. A Facilities & Streets Committee meeting on private roads followed immediately after (outside this pipeline's tracked scope).
Key Decisions
Motion to adjourn approved by show of hands, none opposed. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
